deed: Chaim Weizmann developed a fermentation process for producing acetone that supplied Britain with explosives in World War I
title: Chaim Weizmann developed a fermentation that turned maize into acetone for Britain's explosives in World War I

trailer.text: Chaim Weizmann, later the first President of the State of Israel, was a chemist in Manchester.

In 1914, Britain was in desperate need of large amounts of acetone, which was used to pre-treat gunpowder, and because of the war its supply to Britain from Germany, Russia and Finland was completely stopped.

According to the Weizmann Institute, in 1915 Weizmann developed a fermentation process that converts starch into acetone and butyl alcohol, with the help of a bacterium that had been isolated earlier.
In June 1916 acetone production by the Weizmann process began at a factory in King's Lynn, and in May 1916 work began on a plant in Canada.
Acetone was a key component in cordite, the smokeless gunpowder of the Allies.

paragraphs.text: In 1914 Britain was in desperate need of large amounts of acetone.
The acetone was used to pre-treat the gunpowder.
It was a key component in cordite, the smokeless gunpowder of the Allies.
According to an article in FEMS, the outbreak of the war created a high demand for acetone for smokeless powder.
According to the Weizmann Institute, in those years acetone was produced in Germany, Russia and Finland, and because of the war its supply to Britain stopped completely.
According to the Weizmann Institute, it was made from calcium acetate imported from Germany, and when the Allies were at war with Germany this was no longer possible.
The existing production method was slow and inefficient, and it required tons of wood.
According to Ynetnews, before the war there was no efficient industrial method for producing acetone.
According to Ynetnews, Chaim Weizmann was born on November 27, 1874, into a large, simple Jewish family in the town of Motol in the Pale of Settlement.
According to McGill, he was a Russian-born chemist who had studied in Germany and Switzerland before coming to the University of Manchester.
Perkin joined the Strange group, which was working on the production of synthetic rubber, and the group hired Weizmann and Auguste Fernbach.
According to the Microbiology Society, in the summer of 1912 Perkin dismissed him over salary disagreements, but Weizmann continued to work on butanol production from starch.
According to an article in FEMS, Weizmann was a chemist by training, and trained himself to become a microbiologist as necessary.

stations.title: A bacterium that turns maize into acetone

paragraphs.text: According to the Microbiology Society, in 1914 Weizmann decided to isolate starch-degrading bacteria from maize meal.
According to the same source, he went through 100 to 150 subcultures, and in March 1915 he patented the strain he had obtained.
The bacterium is called Clostridium acetobutylicum.
According to the Weizmann Institute, with its help Weizmann converted starch into acetone and butyl alcohol.
The method became known as the Weizmann process.
Weizmann's American patent describes heat-resisting bacteria that convert the greater part of the starch in maize or other grain into acetone and butyl alcohol.
According to the patent, the maize solution is sterilized for three to four hours, at a temperature of 130 to 140 degrees and a pressure of 2 to 3 atmospheres.
According to the patent, the fermentation proceeds vigorously for about 36 hours and is completed after about 48 hours.
Weizmann wrote to the British authorities about his fermentation system, and they came to see it.
He demonstrated it to them.
According to Leonard Stein, in February 1915 Weizmann demonstrated to Dr. William Rintoul of Nobel's Explosives a process he had invented for the speedier and more economical production of acetone.
According to McGill, in 1915 C.P. Scott, the editor of the Manchester Guardian, introduced Weizmann to Lloyd George, who was then the Minister of Munitions.
According to the Weizmann Institute, Winston Churchill, then First Lord of the Admiralty, requested that the Weizmann process be used.
According to Ynetnews, Churchill quickly summoned Weizmann to his office in London and entrusted him with a crucial mission.
On September 1, 1915, Weizmann was appointed honorary technical adviser on acetone supplies to the British Admiralty.
In September 1915 Weizmann was also appointed chemical adviser on acetone supplies at the Ministry of Munitions, headed by Lloyd George.
Out of patriotism, Weizmann declined to receive payment for the patent until the end of the war, so as not to appear to profit from wartime needs.
According to the Weizmann Institute, Balfour hired him as a paid adviser on the subject of acetone.
In early 1916 the Weizmann process was scaled up to a 7,000-gallon scale, at the Naval Cordite plant in Holton Heath, Dorset.
This was not immediately successful: seven out of ten fermentations failed.
In 1916 the Admiralty built a factory in Poole, near Wareham, to produce acetone by the Weizmann process, and it began successful operations in early 1917.
In June 1916, after successful trials, acetone production by the Weizmann process began at a factory in King's Lynn.
According to the Microbiology Society, the King's Lynn plant switched to the Weizmann strain in mid-1916, and ran continuously on maize until December 1916.
According to McGill, Weizmann was asked to scale up the process, and within a short time converted a gin distillery to the production of his mixture.
In the latter part of 1915 the option of a plant in Toronto was offered, and in May 1916 work began on the Canadian plant.

According to the Microbiology Society, the Toronto plant operated for 27 months and produced 2,450 tonnes of acetone and 4,900 tonnes of butanol, far beyond the 225 tonnes per year that were required.
When the United States joined World War I, the US Army decided to convert two distilleries in Terre Haute, Indiana, into acetone plants.
According to Ynetnews, many breweries in England and the United States were converted into acetone production plants.
The rapid wartime expansion, from laboratory to industrial scale, was unusual among microbiological processes in industry.
According to an article in FEMS, large-scale industrial production began in 1916, and during the war butanol accumulated as an unwanted by-product and was stored.
According to McGill, Weizmann was an avowed Zionist who asked for British help in establishing a homeland for his people.
According to the Weizmann Institute, British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour asked Weizmann what he wished to receive in return for his contribution to the war effort.
According to McGill, it was Lloyd George, when he became prime minister, who asked Weizmann how he would like to be rewarded.
On November 2, 1917, Balfour wrote what became known as the Balfour Declaration.

According to the Weizmann Institute, the Balfour Declaration of 1917 committed the British government to the establishment of a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine, which was then under Ottoman rule.
The extent to which Weizmann's role at the Admiralty influenced the Balfour Declaration is a matter of debate, but his move to London brought him closer to senior British officials.
According to an article in FEMS, in the first part of the 20th century the acetone-butanol fermentation was the second largest fermentation, surpassed in importance only by the ethanol fermentation.
According to the same article, the importance of microbial processes for producing acetone and butanol declined rapidly after World War II.
According to the Weizmann Institute, the acetone-butanol-ethanol (ABE) fermentation, which today enjoys an industrial renaissance, is based on the Weizmann process.
According to Ynetnews, the bacterium Weizmann discovered is still in use today as a source of clean, sustainable alternative energy.
According to the Weizmann Institute, Weizmann was a perennial inventor and entrepreneur, and held 110 patents.
According to Ynetnews, over his lifetime more than 120 patents were registered in his name.
According to the Weizmann Institute, Weizmann established the Daniel Sieff Institute in 1934, and it was renamed the Weizmann Institute in 1949.
According to another Weizmann Institute article, he came to Palestine in 1933 and established the Daniel Sieff Institute for Scientific Research.
Weizmann earned the honor of serving as the first President of the State of Israel.
According to the Weizmann Institute, he became president in 1949.
According to Ynetnews, Weizmann faced significant criticism from Jews in the Land of Israel and around the world for his collaboration with the British.
According to the same source, he had persistent conflicts with other leaders, including David Ben-Gurion, over the way to realize the Zionist vision.
In 1923 the King's Lynn plant was returned to the company Synthetic Products, which restarted it with the Weizmann strain.
The owners of the Weizmann patent, Commercial Solvents Corporation, sued the company for patent infringement.
According to the Microbiology Society, Mr Kane of the Rainham plant reportedly isolated new acetone- and butanol-producing strains, and in 1912 isolated "strain 160" from barley.
The microbiologist Sir Frederick Andrews testified at the trial, and concluded that strain 160 seemed to be identical to the Weizmann strain.
It was also suggested at the trial that the strain 160 cultures had been contaminated with the Weizmann strain, which had been widely used at King's Lynn during the war.

McGill: it was produced from the distillation of wood, and the best wood for this came from the forests of Europe
